paragraphs: Language models retain key and value information from earlier tokens in a cache. Removing less useful entries can reduce memory requirements and inference latency, but choosing poorly can hurt accuracy. This paper argues that importance scores based on attention weights overlook how token value vectors relate to one another in the model’s representation space.

The proposed method, AnDPro, scores tokens by projecting their value vectors onto an anchor direction: the direction of the output before cache eviction. This makes the existing output a reference for deciding which entries to retain. The approach uses the geometry of value representations to guide selection, connecting token importance to the output that eviction may change.

Across 16 LongBench datasets, AnDPro retains 96.07% of full-cache accuracy with a cache budget of 3.44%. The authors also report a 46.0% budget reduction without sacrificing quality relative to previous leading methods. These results support projection-based selection as an effective way to preserve accuracy under tight cache budgets in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2025-accurate-kv-cache-eviction-.tldr: AnDPro selects cached tokens using value-vector projections, retaining 96.07% of full-cache accuracy with a 3.44% cache budget on LongBench.

paragraphs: Foundation models trained on de-identified electronic health records may still memorize patient information. This paper develops ways to assess that risk in models trained on structured medical records. Its central concern is whether retained information could compromise patient privacy, with particular attention to vulnerable subgroups.

The authors introduce a suite of black-box tests that probe memorization at two levels: embeddings and generated outputs. Examining both broadens the assessment beyond what a model explicitly generates. The framework aims to distinguish useful generalization from harmful memorization in clinically relevant settings, making the privacy implications of retained information central to the evaluation.

The approach is validated on a publicly available EHR foundation model, and the authors release an open-source toolkit for reproducible assessments. The stated contribution is an evaluation framework and its demonstrated application, rather than a quantified claim about how commonly healthcare models expose records. By making the tests reusable, the work supports collaborative investigation of privacy risks in this class of models.
neurips-2025-an-investigation-of-memoriz.tldr: The paper introduces black-box tests for privacy-related memorization in healthcare foundation models, covering both embeddings and generated outputs.

paragraphs: Low-rank optimization reduces the memory needed to train language models by projecting gradients into a smaller subspace and storing optimizer states there. The choice of subspace determines which directions remain available for updates. Existing approaches commonly select the dominant gradient subspace because it preserves the most gradient information in the approximation.

The authors identify a problem with that seemingly sensible choice: during pretraining, the dominant subspace can stop changing. Updates then remain confined to similar directions. This observation separates the quality of a gradient approximation at a particular moment from the usefulness of the resulting sequence of updates throughout training.

The paper proposes importance sampling to select subspaces for low-rank optimization and provides a convergence guarantee that the dominant-subspace approach lacks. In pretraining experiments, the proposed method significantly outperforms previous methods. Together, the theory and empirical results support reconsidering how subspaces are chosen: preserving dominant gradient information alone may produce an overly restricted optimization trajectory.
neurips-2025-breaking-the-frozen-subspac.tldr: Importance sampling improves low-rank language-model pretraining by addressing stagnant update subspaces and providing a convergence guarantee.

paragraphs: A model can match observed human preferences while learning the wrong reason for them. The Deep Value Benchmark tests whether language models carry an underlying value into new choices or instead follow a superficial feature that accompanied it during training. This distinction matters for whether preference learning generalizes human intentions.

The benchmark deliberately correlates values and surface features in training, then separates them at test time. For example, avoiding harm might initially appear with formal language, while justice appears with informal language. Test choices reverse these pairings. The Deep Value Generalization Rate measures the probability that the model follows the underlying value when the familiar surface association no longer applies.

Across nine evaluated models, the average rate is 0.30, and every model performs below chance on this measure. Larger models have slightly lower rates than smaller ones. The dataset underwent three human validation experiments. These findings reveal a weakness in generalizing values under the benchmark’s controlled confounding, providing an interpretable test of one aspect of alignment.
neurips-2025-deep-value-benchmark-measur.tldr: DVB separates values from correlated surface cues and finds below-chance deep-value generalization across nine tested language models.

paragraphs: This paper compares masked diffusion language models with autoregressive models when training data is limited but substantial computation is available. In this setting, training repeatedly revisits the same examples. The question is which modeling approach makes better use of those repeated passes, rather than which benefits most from continually receiving fresh data.

The authors find that diffusion models achieve lower validation loss and better downstream performance in this regime. They explain the advantage through randomized masking: diffusion training exposes the model to a varied distribution of token orderings. This provides an implicit form of data augmentation that the fixed left-to-right ordering of autoregressive training does not offer.

The paper also identifies scaling laws for diffusion models and derives a closed-form expression for the compute threshold where diffusion begins to outperform autoregression. Its conclusion is conditional on the resource balance: masked diffusion is a compelling alternative when data scarcity is the bottleneck and enough compute is available to benefit from repeated training.
neurips-2025-diffusion-beats-autoregress.tldr: Masked diffusion models outperform autoregressive models in the studied data-scarce, compute-abundant regime by making better use of repeated training data.

paragraphs: Training the same neural network on the same dataset can produce different models because initialization and batching are random. Traditional training data attribution does not rigorously account for this variation. The paper asks how a dataset affects the distribution of model outputs across training runs, expanding attribution beyond a single trained outcome.

The authors formalize this goal as distributional training data attribution. Within that framework, influence functions emerge as a limit of unrolled differentiation, which follows the effects of changes through training steps. This connection does not require restrictive convexity assumptions. It offers a distributional interpretation of an established attribution tool and a new perspective on why it can work in deep learning.

Experiments demonstrate uses of the framework in improving data pruning for vision transformers and identifying influential examples with diffusion models. These applications connect the theoretical reframing to practical dataset decisions. The central contribution is to make training randomness part of the attribution target, so influence concerns how outputs vary across possible training runs.
neurips-2025-distributional-training-dat.tldr: Distributional training data attribution accounts for training randomness and gives influence functions a new interpretation without restrictive convexity assumptions.

paragraphs: Differentially private learning often uses public data for pretraining, tuning, or estimating the balance between privacy and utility. Suitable public tabular data can be difficult to find because tables vary substantially across domains. This paper proposes generating surrogate public data from publicly available descriptions of a table, without accessing sensitive records.

The inputs include column names, variable types, and permitted ranges. Language models turn this information into plausible records through either direct CSV generation or construction of a structural causal model from which records can be sampled. Because generation is independent of sensitive records and uses only public metadata, the surrogate dataset itself consumes no privacy budget.

Experiments show that these datasets can effectively replace conventional public data for pretraining differentially private tabular classifiers. Benefits are more limited for tuning private synthetic-data generators and estimating privacy–utility tradeoffs. The findings support encoding publicly informed statistical assumptions into reusable datasets, while showing that their usefulness depends on the downstream task.
neurips-2025-do-you-really-need-public-d.tldr: LLM-generated tabular data based solely on public metadata can support private learning, with the strongest reported benefits in classifier pretraining.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to reconstruct a continuous signal from a small number of noisy measurements taken over time. The signal is assumed to contain only k frequency components within a bounded frequency range. This structure makes recovery possible with limited samples, but noise complicates how accurately the continuous signal can be interpolated.

The authors develop a framework that decomposes frequencies hierarchically while systematically canceling noise. It yields a polynomial-time algorithm with a provable approximation factor of 3 + √2 + ε. Previous leading algorithms had constants greater than 100, so the new guarantee substantially narrows the stated gap to optimal recovery.

A second, shrinking-range version offers an approximation factor of √2 + ε + c on a subinterval of length (1 − c)T, for some c between zero and one. This sharper guarantee comes with a shorter reconstruction interval. Together, the results improve the theoretical accuracy available from efficient interpolation algorithms and make explicit the benefit associated with restricting the interval.
neurips-2025-efficient-k-sparse-bandlimi.tldr: A hierarchical noise-cancellation framework sharply improves provable approximation factors for efficient sparse band-limited signal interpolation.

paragraphs: Low-Rank Adaptation adjusts foundation models using relatively few trainable parameters, but those parameters can interfere with one another. Mixture-of-experts variants can reduce correlations within a task, yet add routing parameters and remain ineffective against interference when merging models across tasks. FlyLoRA addresses both issues through a design inspired by the fly olfactory circuit.

FlyLoRA activates experts at the level of individual ranks in the up-projection matrix. Its routing is implicit: a fixed, sparse random projection replaces the usual dense trainable down-projection and also performs routing. Combining these roles removes the need for a separate router. The authors attribute reduced interference between tasks to the orthogonality property of random matrices.

Experiments cover general knowledge understanding, scientific question answering, mathematical reasoning, and code generation, with consistent improvements over existing methods. The approach connects task separation with parameter efficiency through the same architectural choice. Its contribution is a LoRA variant that uses sparse random structure to support expert selection while reducing the additional machinery normally associated with routing.
neurips-2025-flylora-boosting-task-decou.tldr: FlyLoRA combines sparse random projections with implicit expert routing to reduce parameter interference and improve adaptation across four evaluated domains.

paragraphs: End-to-end driving systems map sensor inputs directly to planned actions, but one-shot planning can rely too heavily on the scene as it currently appears. SeerDrive starts from the relationship between a vehicle’s future motion and its changing surroundings: scene evolution informs the plan, and the vehicle’s future states can influence how the scene develops.

The framework predicts future bird’s-eye-view representations of the surroundings and supplies those predicted features to the trajectory planner. It then iteratively refines both scene predictions and vehicle plans through collaborative optimization. This creates a feedback process in which the two predictions are developed together instead of treating future scene information as a fixed input.

Experiments on NAVSIM and nuScenes show significant improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods. The results support using anticipated scene dynamics within trajectory generation and refining the two jointly. The contribution is a framework for future-aware planning, with benchmark evidence that accounting for this bidirectional relationship improves end-to-end driving performance.
neurips-2025-future-aware-end-to-end-dri.tldr: SeerDrive jointly refines future scene predictions and driving trajectories, significantly improving performance on NAVSIM and nuScenes.

paragraphs: RNA inverse design seeks sequences compatible with a desired structure. Many sequences can correspond to one RNA three-dimensional structure, making it useful to represent a range of candidates. Existing methods often focus on secondary structure or generate only a limited number of sequences. RBFN combines sequence distribution modeling with richer treatment of three-dimensional geometry.

The method uses a Bayesian Flow Network to model nucleotide sequences and geometric algebra to strengthen its representation of RNA structure. The geometric component addresses the flexibility of RNA conformations. The authors also introduce a time-step sampling distribution intended to address the scarcity of RNA structural data and the small alphabet of four nucleotide types.

Evaluations on single-state and multi-state fixed-backbone benchmarks indicate that RBFN can outperform existing RNA design methods across various tasks. These results support the combination of distribution-based sequence generation and geometric structural modeling for effective RNA design. The evidence concerns sequences designed against specified backbones, including settings involving one structural state and settings involving multiple states.
neurips-2025-geometric-algebra-enhanced-.tldr: RBFN combines Bayesian sequence generation and geometric structural modeling to improve RNA design on single-state and multi-state fixed-backbone benchmarks.

paragraphs: A formal proof can be syntactically valid while the system producing it still struggles to recognize reusable mathematical structure. Ineq-Comp investigates this issue through inequalities, asking whether automated provers can identify familiar results and combine them within a larger solution. The focus is compositional reasoning rather than simply solving an isolated elementary inequality.

The benchmark transforms elementary problems through variable duplication, algebraic rewriting, and combinations requiring several inequality applications. Most evaluated provers struggle on these variants despite their remaining easy for humans. DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B is relatively robust but still shows a 20% drop in pass@32, the reported measure based on multiple proof attempts.

A gap between seed problems and compositional variants also persists for DeepSeek-Prover-V2-671B, indicating that scaling alone does not fully resolve the tested weakness. Providing formal proofs of the component inequalities in context still leaves all models performing poorly. That finding points to difficulty assembling known pieces into a solution, beyond simply having access to the constituent results.
neurips-2025-ineq-comp-benchmarking-huma.tldr: Ineq-Comp reveals persistent difficulty combining elementary inequalities, even in large theorem provers supplied with proofs of the component results.

paragraphs: Treatment-effect models may be trained on detailed, structured patient information but later receive only a textual description, such as self-reported symptoms. These descriptions can omit information present during training. The paper shows that this mismatch can bias treatment-effect estimates, making the representation available at prediction time a central part of the estimation problem.

The authors formalize the mismatch as inference-time text confounding. In their setting, confounders are fully observed during training but only partially represented in the text available during inference. The issue therefore persists even when the training dataset contains the relevant variables: the prediction interface supplies an incomplete account of them.

To address this, the proposed framework combines language models with a custom doubly robust learner that explicitly accounts for the text-confounding problem. Experiments demonstrate effectiveness in real-world applications. The contribution is both a formal description of an overlooked source of bias and a method intended to mitigate it when structured training information must support predictions from incomplete text.
neurips-2025-llm-driven-treatment-effect.tldr: The paper identifies bias from incomplete inference-time patient text and proposes an LLM-assisted doubly robust framework to mitigate it.

paragraphs: Multi-agent reinforcement learning often approximates a global value function by adding local value functions, one for each agent’s state. This decomposition is widely useful, but its theoretical basis has received less attention. The paper identifies a mathematical property of state transitions that determines when such a decomposition is possible.

The authors call this property Markov entanglement, drawing an analogy with quantum entanglement. They establish that an MDP permits value decomposition if and only if its transition matrix is not entangled in their sense. They also introduce a measure of entanglement that bounds decomposition error in general multi-agent MDPs, connecting exact decomposability with the quality of approximate decompositions.

For the widely used class of index policies, the authors prove weak entanglement and a decomposition-error bound scaling as O(√N) for N agents. This grows sublinearly with the number of agents. They further show that entanglement can be estimated efficiently, providing a practical way to assess whether value decomposition is a suitable approximation for a system.
neurips-2025-multi-agent-markov-entangle.tldr: Markov entanglement characterizes when multi-agent values decompose and provides error bounds, including O(√N) scaling for index policies.

paragraphs: Protein structure predictors can produce accurate three-dimensional hypotheses from sequence, yet often miss the range of conformations adopted by dynamic molecular complexes. Cryo-electron microscopy can reveal structural heterogeneity, but converting its experimental data into atomic models requires demanding processing. CryoBoltz combines these complementary sources of structural information.

The method guides a pretrained biomolecular predictor during inference using constraints derived from cryo-EM density maps. It applies both global and local constraints along the model’s sampling trajectory, steering predictions toward conformations consistent with the experiment. The predictor contributes learned sequence and biophysical information, while the density map provides evidence about the structural states present in the measured system.

The authors demonstrate atomic-model construction in heterogeneous maps across dynamic biomolecular systems, including transporters and antibodies. These examples support inference-time guidance as a way to connect structure prediction with experimentally observed conformational diversity. The method’s role is to make structural hypotheses responsive to density-map evidence while drawing on the capabilities already learned by the pretrained predictor.
neurips-2025-multiscale-guidance-of-prot.tldr: CryoBoltz guides a pretrained structure predictor with global and local cryo-EM constraints to build atomic models of experimentally observed conformations.

paragraphs: Online change detection asks whether the distribution producing a data stream has shifted, using observations as they arrive. This paper addresses multivariate streams without imposing a parametric distribution model. It frames detection as a sequence of kernel-based two-sample tests and uses random Fourier features to make the procedure computationally efficient.

The algorithm requires neither a training dataset known to come from the pre-change distribution nor a user-selected window for local tests. These properties matter when a reliable baseline is unavailable and choosing a comparison horizon would otherwise become another tuning decision. The procedure uses logarithmic time per observation and logarithmic overall storage.

The authors prove performance guarantees, including information-theoretic bounds establishing minimax-optimal detection delay. This gives a worst-case optimality statement within the analyzed problem setting. Numerical studies on synthetic and real data show competitive performance against the state of the art. The work thus combines efficient streaming operation, reduced setup requirements, and theoretical control over how quickly a change can be detected.
neurips-2025-optimal-online-change-detec.tldr: A random-Fourier-feature detector achieves minimax-optimal delay with logarithmic time and space, without pre-change training data or a user-set window.

paragraphs: Interactive tasks such as negotiation require language models to consider consequences across multiple turns. Reinforcement-learning fine-tuning can support planning, but multi-turn training is expensive, and the largest API-based models may lack the interfaces it requires. This paper proposes guiding the agent’s reasoning with learned value functions that remain usable with such models.

These functions are conditioned on goals and predict how a task may unfold following an action. They let an agent assess possible positive and negative outcomes while deciding how to proceed. Training operates over reasoning steps rather than full actions, producing a concise, lightweight component for decision-making during interactions.

The method is evaluated on tool use, social deduction, and dialogue. The authors report superior performance to both reinforcement-learning fine-tuning and prompting approaches while retaining efficiency and scalability. The findings support learned value guidance as a practical way to improve interactive planning, including for large models accessed through APIs, without requiring the expensive policy-training setup described in the paper.
neurips-2025-planning-without-search-ref.tldr: Goal-conditioned value functions guide language-model reasoning and improve interactive planning across tool use, social deduction, and dialogue tasks.

paragraphs: Random walk neural networks represent graphs by processing sampled walks with sequence models. Under realistic sampling budgets, walks may miss nodes and edges, leaving the model without important global structure. Random search neural networks replace these walks with searches that each guarantee coverage of every node.

For sparse graphs, the authors prove that O(log |V|) searches suffice for full edge coverage, compared with O(|V|) walks when walk lengths scale with graph size. They also establish universal approximation when the searches are paired with universal sequence models. A further result shows probabilistic invariance to graph isomorphisms: the expected output is unchanged by an isomorphic representation of the graph.

On molecular and protein benchmarks, RSNNs consistently outperform random walk networks, obtaining comparable or better performance with up to 16 times fewer sampled sequences. The empirical and theoretical findings both support improving what each sampled sequence covers. The coverage advantage is especially relevant to sparse graphs, the setting of the stated sampling-complexity result.
neurips-2025-random-search-neural-networ.tldr: Random search neural networks improve graph coverage and expressivity, matching or exceeding random-walk performance with up to 16 times fewer sequences.

paragraphs: Training-free neural architecture search ranks candidate networks at initialization using proxy scores, avoiding the need to train each candidate. Those scores are often designed manually, requiring expertise and substantial effort. The paper also identifies weak correlation with final performance and high computational cost as problems with existing handcrafted proxies.

Automatic Proxy Discovery, or APD, uses language models to generate these scoring methods. It adds actor-critic reinforcement learning to optimize the prompts used for subsequent generations of proxies. This creates an iterative discovery process in which prompt improvement is intended to produce better proxy candidates, automating part of the algorithm-design work behind architecture search.

Experiments on mainstream architecture-search benchmarks demonstrate strong performance and efficiency. The practical contribution is therefore a method for discovering the inexpensive evaluators on which training-free search depends. The results support using language models within proxy design, with reinforcement learning helping direct later generations, rather than treating the proxy as a fixed manually supplied component.
neurips-2025-revolutionizing-training-fr.tldr: APD uses language models and reinforcement-learning prompt optimization to automatically discover effective proxies for training-free neural architecture search.

paragraphs: Federated learning must combine training across participants whose data distributions can differ substantially. Prior approaches often restrict local updates using global information as the standard for agreement. This paper argues that such hard consensus can make it difficult to balance useful local features with information shared across participants.

The proposed method pursues soft consensus through multiple solution paths that accommodate different preferences for local and global features. These paths are combined through a negotiation process directed at the same objective. Because local features can dominate local training, the method uses a swapping strategy to weaken that dominance and better balance the paths.

Multiple paths could increase communication requirements. To reduce parameter transmission, the authors convert the task-network solution into data adaptation. Extensive experiments demonstrate advantages for the proposed method. Its contribution is a coordinated approach to heterogeneous federated learning: negotiate between local and global feature preferences, counteract local dominance, and address the additional communication introduced by pursuing multiple paths.
neurips-2025-soft-consensual-federated-l.tldr: The method balances local and global information through multiple negotiated solution paths while reducing their added communication cost.

paragraphs: Low-rank approximation retains a matrix’s leading structure, but noise can alter the approximation itself. This paper measures that change using the spectral norm, which captures the largest error in any direction. That perspective matters when aggregate reconstruction measures fail to reflect how strongly particular directions have been distorted.

The authors derive high-probability perturbation bounds for symmetric matrices that explicitly account for interactions between the original matrix and a symmetric perturbation. Under mild eigengap and norm conditions, the bounds sharpen estimates of the difference between the original and perturbed rank-p approximations, with improvements of up to a factor of √n. Their analysis uses a new contour bootstrapping method from complex analysis.

Applied to differentially private PCA, the results improve utility guarantees and resolve an open problem identified in the literature. The analysis also extends to spectral functions such as matrix polynomials and exponentials. Experiments on real-world datasets show that the bounds closely follow measured spectral errors across diverse perturbations, connecting the theoretical refinements to observed behavior.
neurips-2025-spectral-perturbation-bound.tldr: Sharper spectral perturbation bounds improve guarantees for low-rank approximation and private PCA under stated eigengap and norm conditions.

paragraphs: Time-series foundation models face shortages and imbalances in training data. This paper addresses those problems by generating synthetic time series together with corresponding symbolic expressions. Inspired by theories of complex dynamical systems, the generation mechanism is designed to produce high-quality paired data without being restricted to an existing collection of recorded series.

The authors build SymTime, a pretrained model that uses the strong relationship between a series and its symbolic counterpart to improve time-series representations. The paired format is central: it supplies symbolic information alongside the numerical sequence during pretraining. The work therefore combines a data-generation mechanism with a model designed to benefit from the resulting pairs.

After fine-tuning on downstream tasks, SymTime achieves competitive performance across five major time-series analysis tasks, rivaling foundation models pretrained on real-world datasets. These findings support synthetic series-symbol pairs as a useful pretraining resource. They suggest that generated data and associated symbolic information can help address data scarcity while supporting performance across multiple downstream analyses.
neurips-2025-synthetic-series-symbol-dat.tldr: SymTime learns from synthetic time series paired with symbolic expressions and rivals real-data-pretrained models across five tasks after fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Some observations of English-like internal activations have suggested that multilingual language models might think in English. This paper investigates a different explanation: a compact set of parameters supports abilities shared across languages. The authors find that deactivating this small parameter subset substantially degrades performance across all languages examined.

They identify neurons consistently active for particular languages and distinguish shared neurons from language-exclusive ones. As models develop, shared neurons increase in both proportion and functional importance, while exclusive neurons become less influential. The authors interpret this pattern as the emergence of a language-agnostic core supporting abstraction beyond a particular linguistic system.

These observations motivate neuron-specific training strategies matched to a model’s degree of language independence at different developmental stages. Experiments across multiple model families support the approach. The work connects internal activation patterns, the consequences of parameter deactivation, and targeted training, offering evidence for shared multilingual processing and a practical way to use that evidence when designing training strategies.
neurips-2025-the-emergence-of-abstract-t.tldr: The authors identify a small, increasingly important multilingual parameter core and use its properties to motivate neuron-specific training strategies.

paragraphs: Time-series forecasting models often devote most of their design effort to understanding historical observations. The paper focuses instead on how they construct future predictions. Predicting multiple future time points separately may fail to capture patterns spanning the forecast, especially when the series combines short-term and long-term dynamics.

Implicit Forecaster is an additional decoding module that represents the forecast through constituent waves. It implicitly predicts their frequencies, amplitudes, and phases, then forms the time series from those components. This connects future values through shared wave descriptions, providing a way to express structure across the forecast rather than handling each predicted time point independently.

Experiments on several real-world datasets show consistent improvements when the module is added to mainstream time-series models, with resulting state-of-the-art forecasting performance. The findings support decoding as an important source of forecasting gains alongside historical-series modeling. The contribution is a reusable forecasting component that translates predicted wave properties into a structured sequence of future values.
neurips-2025-towards-accurate-time-serie.tldr: Implicit Forecaster improves time-series models by decoding future sequences through constituent waves defined by frequency, amplitude, and phase.

paragraphs: Temporal vision-language models must understand changes across images, but they may rely on static cues such as objects or backgrounds. These shortcuts can produce systematic classification errors. TRoVe is designed to discover which static features contribute to those failures in an already trained model.

Given a trained model and an annotated validation dataset, TRoVe extracts candidate static features and scores them on two dimensions: their effect on classification errors and the model’s reliance on them when predicting. This connects a feature’s association with mistakes to evidence that it influences the model’s decisions. The method specifically targets failure analysis in temporal tasks.

The authors introduce an evaluation framework with 101 trained temporal models and ground-truth annotations of learned biases. TRoVe improves by 28.6% over the closest baseline in that evaluation. Applying it to seven off-the-shelf models on two temporal tasks reveals previously unknown biases. The authors also demonstrate that knowledge of those biases can help improve test-time performance, linking diagnosis to a practical benefit.
neurips-2025-trove-discovering-error-ind.tldr: TRoVe identifies static visual shortcuts behind temporal-model errors and demonstrates that discovering these biases can help improve test-time performance.
